103.t: The Billie Holiday date with Benny Goodman and Freddie Green joining
103.s: He recalls a January 1937 Billie Holiday recording with Goodman, Teddy Wilson and the Basie men, after which Freddie Green joined the band.
103.q: If we did anything when we was at the Roseland for a month - if there was anything that he played that month, I would have to try to find some old dir shots that was made in 1936 coming into the first 2 weeks of January, because 'round about January the 17th or 18th we made a recording with Benny…

103.t: How the Teddy Wilson sessions drew on whichever band was in town
103.s: Hinton explains that the personnel came from the stars of whatever band was in New York, and Jones cites the January 30, 1939 session.
103.ch: Billie Holiday and the band's singers
103.q: That's right, January the 30th, 1939, see, because you remember at that time I told you that we had been to the Famous Door and that's when Cozy joined Cab, 'cause we were there thirty 5 1/2 months. We were on 52nd Street.

103.t: Bill Pemberton asks about the Teddy Wilson sessions
103.s: Pemberton asks about mixing men from different orchestras, and Jones says they were just trying to get a point across, not be commercial.
103.ch: Billie Holiday and the band's singers
103.q: Later on we had called the Roseland and there then were some dates. As you know, you played on the dates because we were out of town.

103.t: Billie Holiday joins Basie; the January 1937 record date
103.s: Jones explains why the band wanted a woman singer, and gives January 25, 1937 for the first Teddy Wilson date with Billie Holiday and the Basie men.
103.ch: Billie Holiday and the band's singers
103.q: I run into Billie - now we got Jimmie Rushing, so now we're tired of going out on the road with a bunch of men, so we got to have a vocalist. A girl, got to have some woman there, you know what I mean, because if we got a woman in the group at least we can get some rooming houses, if we got a woman…

383.t: Billie Holiday recording sessions with Hammond
383.s: Wilson explains Hammond's all-star sessions for Brunswick and then Columbia, using whoever was in town including Hinton.
383.ch: Joining Carter and Goodman in New York
383.q: Right, the Holiday session started, and John Hammond set those up with Brunswick Records in 1935, and then when Brunswick went out of business, it concentrated on bowling and billiard balls, the stock was sold to Columbia, and we continued right on with Columbia with Billie singing, these small…

383.t: The Billie Holiday session musicians and their classic records
383.s: Wilson lists the many players on the Holiday dates and agrees records like 'Miss Brown to You' were never surpassed; Goodman played under a phony name.
383.q: more excited about the musicians we had on those dates than I was about Billie, because we had Johnny Hodges, whom I'd been idolizing for years; Benny Carter, Lester Young was on, Chu Berry, Bud Freeman did a lot of them. Benny Goodman was on clarinet on a lot of them, Ben Webster on tenor, Roy…

92.t: Recording with Billie Holiday, Prez and Una Mae Carlisle
92.s: Collins names players he recorded with, including a late-night date with Billie and Lester Young and Victor sides with Una Mae Carlisle that were never promoted.
92.ch: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
92.q: Let's see, Bill Doggett, Billie Holiday, Roy, Don -- Redman, Art, just to name a few. It's just-- you know, it was -- I was playing with Roy, and at the -- I think it was the -- it was Kelly's Stables and we recorded with -- Billie wanted us to record with her so we recorded after we got off that…

92.t: Recording with Mildred Bailey in Chicago and New York
92.s: Bailey wanted Roy Eldridge, Teddy Wilson and Collins on her dates, recorded with the Three Deuces band in Chicago, and gave parties for musicians.
92.ch: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
92.q: And I might add that during this same time I was doing quite a bit of recording with Mildred Bailey. She kept -- she always wanted Roy, Teddy Wilson and myself with her. It's a marvelous dates because we did some things with I think the writer was Alec Wilder, and she did some very good things…

473.t: Recording behind Billie Holiday with Teddy Wilson's studio groups
473.s: He and Cozy Cole recorded often with Billie Holiday under Teddy Wilson (Brunswick or Vocalion), with Goodman, Hodges, Carney, Ben Webster and later Lester Young sitting in on dates.
473.q: Broadway. And we'd have -- sometimes Benny Goodman would be on the date and sometimes Allen Reuss And we'd change around. Sometimes we'd have Johnny Hodges, Harry Carney, sometimes they'd have Ben Webster.

473.t: Cozy Cole joins the Onyx band and Billie Holiday sessions
473.s: Johnnie Washington was the first drummer; Cozy Cole came in a few months later, and they hung out together and went to hear Billie before recording with her, including Red Allen on a Billie session.
473.q: No. We had a little guy named Johnnie Washington. He stayed with us for about, oh, three or four months, in the Onyx. And then we brought in Cozy.

400.t: Six months at the Cotton Club and recording on the side despite Cab's ban
400.s: Cab did not want his men recording with others, but Ben Webster threatened to leave, so Hinton made sessions with Teddy Wilson and Billie Holiday.
400.ch: Cab Calloway's band: road, arrangers and shows
400.q: It was as best it possibly could be at that time. He was insisting… Cab Calloway… first we do six months in the Cotton Club, which is a long time.

406.t: Freelance sessions while on staff, including the unreleased Billie Holiday Story
406.s: He played sessions with Red Allen, Max Kaminsky, Hackett, Armstrong and others, and later played on Chaney Scott's Billie Holiday Story, withheld after a lawsuit, around 1960.
406.q: Then in the meantime in the radio station you had other opportunities to play other places. And I played, you know, with every -- all of the sessions and things that were around. Then I did some work with -- I played with Red Allen. I was with Red Allen quite a bit. We played Max Kamansky and Bobby…

17.t: Billie Holiday's first records; 'Sweethearts on Parade' with Hampton and Chu Berry
17.s: Cole recalls the early Billie Holiday and Teddy Wilson sessions and a Hampton record with Chu Berry.
17.ch: Stuff Smith, 52nd Street and session work
17.q: Oh great, great. See, we made some of those first recordings with Billie, "Miss Brown to You," and "What Living Moonlight Can Do," with Korby, Ben, I think it was Benny Goodman and Billy Taylor, Teddy Wilson, Artie Shaw on on some of them, wasn't he? I just forget now. But we all made those first…

67.t: Joining Teddy Wilson's band with singer Jean Eldridge
67.s: Back in October 1939 he joined Teddy Wilson, recording with vocalist Jean Eldridge, with Ben Webster, Al Casey and Harold Baker nearby.
67.ch: Teddy Wilson, Cafe Society and bebop
67.q: Jean Eldridge was a very fine girl. I think she would've been as big as Billie Holiday, if she had stuck with her profession. She was a great singer and she

73.t: First recording date with Billie Holiday and Lester Young
73.s: Days later he arrived first at the studio and recorded with Billie, Teddy Wilson, Lester, Buck Clayton and Jo Jones.
73.q: And, I think the next day, or two days later, or something like that I had a recording date. You know, they said "Why don't you go down to the studio" -- some studio -- I forgot what studio.

115.t: Session work in New York: Billie Holiday and the Ink Spots
115.s: While with Vinson he played dates with Billie Holiday, Roy Eldridge and the Ink Spots, arranged through Mo Gale.
115.ch: Postwar: Chicago, Vinson, Hines and Cootie
115.q: Well, maybe with Cleanhead. No, I could have been with Cleanhead. No, no, I was doing record dates with other groups around New York.

428.t: Recording with Johnny Hodges and Billie Holiday
428.s: Hall recalls Hodges sessions and his only Billie Holiday date, led by Don Redman.
428.q: Yeah, it was in, that was about '40, 1940, or '41. That's the only date I did with her.. Don Redman was the leader of the band with Jimmy Hamilton and George (inaudible) and Don Byas and J. C. Herd, Roy Eldrige.

124.t: Teddy Wilson sessions with Billie Holiday
124.s: Welburn reads the personnel of the January 1936 Teddy Wilson session with Billie Holiday and a March date.
124.ch: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
124.q: Teddy Wilson and his orchestra, Gordon Griffin, trumpet, Rudy Powell, yourself, Teddy, John True hart again, Grachan Moncure the second on bass, and Cozy and Billie Holiday.

79.s: Thomas spent about a year in Teddy Wilson's sextet at Cafe Society, with Benny Morton, Edmond Hall and Sid Catlett, and recorded V-Discs during the Petrillo recording ban.
79.ch: The 1940s: small groups, Teddy Wilson and Ethel Waters
79.q: Oh, yeah. There was Teddy, of course. ... Benny Morton is on this side, there's Joe Thomas, trumpet player and Edmond me, Edward Hall, Sidney Catlett and Johnny Wilson. And, that was during the time of a record strike. Petrillo had called a record strike and we couldn't record at all. But, we did…
